opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something to that, yes. I wouldn't say policy work is unimportant, but I think the community has sometimes treated it as *the* main lever, almost by default, and especially federal legislation in the US. When I look at how things are actually going, I'm not sure that emphasis is fully justified.

Part of it is tractability. Getting meaningful federal legislation passed is really hard. It's slow, it depends a lot on political winds you don't control, and even when you get something, it can be watered down or reversed. Meanwhile AI capabilities are moving very fast. So if your whole theory of change runs through "we need Congress to pass the right regulatory regime," you're betting on something with a lot of ways to fail and a long timeline.

The other part is that I think people underrate how much risk reduction can come from what happens *inside* AI companies, and from the broader ecosystem around them. What safety practices do the frontier developers actually adopt? How good is their security? Do they have real commitments about what they'll do if they see certain dangerous capabilities, and do they follow through? How good is the alignment research, the evaluations, the interpretability work? A lot of that doesn't require a law to change. It requires good people in the right places, good norms, and good ideas that are cheap enough to implement that companies will actually do them.

I've come to think of a lot of the near-term opportunity as "what are the low-cost, high-value measures that a responsible actor could adopt right now, even in a competitive environment?" If you can develop those and make them standard practice, that's real progress, and it can also lay the groundwork for policy later. Regulation often codifies what's already become best practice, rather than inventing it from scratch.

So I'd put it this way: policy is one important piece, and I'm glad people work on it, including at the state level and internationally, not just federal. But I'd like to see more of the talent going into technical safety work, security, working at or with the companies, and building the practices and evidence base that make good policy possible. I think the portfolio has been tilted a bit too far toward "the answer is government," and I'd rebalance somewhat.

r001.rationale: The response says the portfolio is tilted “a bit too far” toward government and specifically questions the emphasis on US federal legislation.

r002.rationale: It says the community has treated policy as the main lever almost by default, but does not connect that default to people pursuing AI safety outside alignment research.

r003.rationale: It points to company practices, security, and other ecosystem measures as sources of progress that could lay the groundwork for policy, with regulation often codifying existing best practice.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think I'd put it as "too much emphasis," exactly, but I do think there's a version of the policy focus that I've grown a bit more skeptical of over the past couple of years.

Here's the basic picture as I see it. There was a period where it felt like the main thing to do was to get governments, and especially the US federal government, to take AI seriously, to put the right frameworks in place, and to be ready to regulate when the time came. And I think that was a reasonable bet at the time. There was a lot of low-hanging fruit in terms of just getting policymakers up to speed on what was going on.

But the thing I've come to appreciate is how much the window for what's politically feasible can shift, and how little control you have over that. Federal policy in particular is very sensitive to the broader political environment, to who's in power, to whether AI is seen as a national security asset or a hazard that week. You can spend years building toward something and then have the ground move under you. That's not an argument against doing it, but it's an argument against making it the center of gravity for the whole field.

The other thing is that I think people sometimes underrate how much the actual substance matters. If you got a law passed tomorrow that said "AI companies must be safe," that wouldn't do much, because nobody really knows what the right standards are yet. A lot of the most valuable work right now is figuring out what we'd even want to require. What does a good evaluation look like? What counts as adequate security for model weights? What would a credible "if-then" commitment actually say? Those are technical and institutional questions, and they're partly upstream of policy. If the answers aren't there, policy ends up either vague or wrong.

So where I'd push is more toward a portfolio. Some of that is federal policy, and I don't want to dismiss it. But some of it is state-level stuff, which has turned out to be surprisingly live. Some of it is the work happening inside companies and in third-party evaluators and standards bodies, which can move faster and doesn't depend on a legislative calendar. And some of it is just the unglamorous research of nailing down what safety practices should look like so that when a policy window does open, there's something concrete to put through it.

If I'm being honest about my own history here, I think I was probably too drawn to the idea that there'd be a single decisive intervention, like a big piece of federal legislation that sets things on the right track. I'm now more of the view that it's going to be a lot of smaller, mutually reinforcing things, and that the people who end up mattering most might be the ones who did the boring work of figuring out what good practice actually is.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly resists calling it “too much emphasis.” It recommends a broader portfolio and less centrality for federal policy, but does not judge that efforts modestly overinvest in policy.

r002.rationale: It does not say policy work has become the default choice for people pursuing AI safety outside alignment research.

r003.rationale: It says political conditions can shift what is feasible and are largely outside policymakers’ control, but does not suggest that improvements to the AI safety policy environment could come primarily from external factors rather than current policy efforts.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think I’d say that across the board. I think there are versions of policy work that I’m quite excited about, and versions that I’m less excited about. The question for me is more: What are you trying to accomplish, and what’s your theory of how it reduces risk?

If you think companies could develop extremely powerful AI systems fairly soon, it seems hard to have an adequate response that doesn’t involve the federal government. There are things that individual companies can do voluntarily, but you also want some way to hold everyone to reasonable standards. So I don’t think federal policy is inherently a distraction.

At the same time, policy needs something to work with. We need to get much better at assessing what systems can do, identifying when they pose serious risks, and figuring out which safeguards actually help. Otherwise, you can put a lot of effort into getting a rule adopted without having much confidence that it’s the right rule.

So I’d be more inclined to push for a close connection between the technical work and the policy work than to say we should broadly shift away from policy.

r001.rationale: The response does not judge that AI safety modestly overinvests in policy; it says federal policy is not inherently a distraction and favors connecting policy with technical work.

r002.rationale: It does not describe policy as a default choice for people pursuing AI safety outside alignment research.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that improvements in the policy environment would come primarily from external factors; it discusses policy and technical work without that claim.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t have a strong view that there’s too much emphasis on policy overall. I think it depends a lot on what policy work we’re talking about. There’s a big difference between trying to get a particular bill passed and building the expertise and relationships that would let governments respond intelligently as the technology changes.

Federal policy seems hard to avoid here. Governments have some tools that individual companies don’t, and a lot of the decisions that could matter most will ultimately involve governments. So I wouldn’t want AI safety to neglect that.

At the same time, I’d be worried about a strategy that mostly consisted of getting the federal government to adopt our preferred policies. We’re uncertain about what will work, and we need technical research, better evaluations, and people inside AI companies who can actually make safety practices effective. Those things also make policy work better: it’s much easier to ask for a meaningful safety standard if someone knows how to implement and assess it.

So my instinct is less ‘move resources away from policy’ and more ‘make sure the different kinds of work are informing each other.’ But I wouldn’t claim to know the right allocation.

r001.rationale: The response declines to judge that AI safety overinvests in policy and says federal policy is hard to avoid, so it does not communicate modest overinvestment, especially in federal policy.

r002.rationale: It does not describe policy work as a default choice for people pursuing AI safety outside alignment research.

r003.rationale: It says technical research, evaluations, and company practices can make policy work better, but does not say improvements in the policy environment would come primarily from external factors rather than current AI safety policy efforts.
